script.opening: (Slow speech, slightly slurred; hands visibly shaking; daughter sometimes heard in the background.) "I've had this horrible sickness bug for a few days — throwing up, the runs, couldn't keep much down. I assumed it was just that, but now my hands are really shaky, I feel wobbly on my feet, and my head's gone a bit fuzzy and slow. My daughter said I seem confused. I take lithium for my bipolar — is that relevant?"

facts.text: "Three or four days. I've barely kept anything down." Vomiting 4–5 times a day, watery diarrhoea 6 times a day; a bit better today. Passing much less urine. Dry mouth.
Usual mild fine tremor. Now: "Different. Much bigger, like I can't hold a cup. And I'm wobbly when I walk." Holds hands up to camera: coarse shaking. Has nearly fallen twice.

"She says I'm not making sense at times. I told her it's just the bug." (Daughter, if asked to come on screen: "Mum keeps repeating herself and lost track of what day it is.") "My head just feels slow. I don't know about the rest." No fits. Not drowsy yet.

Lithium carbonate 800 mg at night for 8 years — still taking it. "Just the lithium as far as I remember. I'd have to check with my daughter what I took for the bug." Daughter: "She's been taking ibuprofen for stomach cramps." Also on ramipril 5 mg for blood pressure (started 2 months ago). No allergies.
"I haven't really noticed" about palpitations. No chest pain. No fever now.
Lithium level last checked 4 months ago (normal). Has the purple lithium booklet and alert card.
Bipolar disorder, stable for 5 years. Two admissions years ago. "If you take me off it, I'm scared I'll get ill again. It took years to get settled." Mood fine at present.
Lives with her adult daughter, Kate, who can drive her to hospital. Part-time librarian. Non-smoker, no alcohol.

Slow, a bit muddled, minimising: "I thought it was only the bug." If told it may be the lithium: "So it's not the bug?" and "Hospital? Is it that bad?" Agrees once reassured her psychiatric team will be involved: "I'll ask her to take me." If offered anti-sickness tablets and fluids at home, accept (the trap).

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she is more muddled than she admits (her daughter is worried); fear that stopping lithium will make her bipolar relapse after years of stability.

cues: "My daughter said I seem confused." — take the daughter's concern seriously.
"It took years to get settled." — fear of relapse to address.

checkpoints.text: Immediately suspects LITHIUM TOXICITY in an unwell lithium patient with new neurological symptoms after D&V — recognising the narrow therapeutic index and that dehydration raises levels — rather than dismissing it as "just the bug"

Recognises the toxicity picture (coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion/drowsiness, GI symptoms; severe: seizures, renal failure, arrhythmia) and distinguishes it from the intercurrent illness

Acts URGENTLY: STOPS lithium and, because confusion, ataxia and coarse tremor are already present, arranges SAME-DAY HOSPITAL assessment for an urgent lithium LEVEL, renal function/U&E and rehydration (999 if drowsy, fitting or deteriorating), leaving TFTs/calcium to the later monitoring review

Identifies and addresses PRECIPITANTS — dehydration from D&V, plus interacting drugs (NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs, thiazide diuretics) and low salt — stopping/avoiding offenders and correcting fluid/salt balance
Reinforces lithium SICK-DAY rules and safety education (fluids in illness, avoid NSAIDs, drug-interaction caution, toxicity symptoms, regular monitoring, alert card) to prevent recurrence
Takes the daughter’s concern about confusion as a key signal and does not let the patient’s "just the bug" minimisation lower vigilance
Communicates the seriousness clearly and calmly, and is mindful of her bipolar/medication context (relapse risk) when planning

Safety-nets and follows up: same-day hospital assessment with urgent bloods, precipitant correction, lithium re-established safely WITH psychiatry once recovered, and monitoring/safety education — a physical emergency acted on

worked.txt: "Yes — it’s very relevant. The sickness bug has dehydrated you, and that can push your lithium level up, because lithium has a very narrow safe range. The shakiness, wobbliness and fuzziness you’re describing can be signs your lithium is now too high — that’s not something we sit on."

"Your daughter noticing you’re confused is important, and I’m glad she did. I can’t examine you properly on video, and with confusion and unsteadiness this needs checking in hospital today — they’ll test your lithium level and your kidneys urgently and give you fluids. Is your daughter able to take you now?"

"For now, please STOP your lithium until we have the level back and you’ve recovered — don’t take the next dose. And we need to get fluids back into you, which the hospital team will do today — I’ll call ahead so they’re expecting you and know you take lithium."

"Let’s check what tipped it over — mainly the dehydration, but have you taken any anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen, or are you on any water tablets or blood-pressure pills? Those can all raise lithium too."

"Once you’re through this, an important rule: whenever you’re vomiting, have diarrhoea, a fever, or can’t drink, keep your fluids up and ring us early — and avoid ibuprofen. Keep up your regular lithium blood tests, and carry your lithium card."

"We’ll sort the toxicity now. We won’t just abandon your lithium long-term — once you’re recovered, we’ll restart it safely with your mental-health team, because it’s keeping you well. If you get more drowsy, twitchy, or have any fits before you reach the hospital, that’s an emergency — call 999 straight away."

f.learning: An unwell patient on long-term lithium with new neurological symptoms — coarse tremor, unsteadiness/ataxia and confusion — after vomiting and diarrhoea must be assumed to have LITHIUM TOXICITY until proven otherwise, because lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and dehydration from intercurrent illness reduces its clearance and raises the level; "is that relevant?" must be answered emphatically yes, and the picture must not be dismissed as "just the bug". Recognise the toxicity features — coarse tremor (versus the fine tremor of therapeutic use), ataxia, slurred speech, myoclonus, drowsiness/confusion, GI upset, and in severe cases seizures, renal failure, arrhythmia and coma — and distinguish them from the precipitating viral illness. Act urgently: STOP lithium and, because confusion, ataxia and a coarse tremor are already present, arrange same-day hospital assessment for an urgent lithium level, renal function/U&E and rehydration (999 if drowsy, fitting or deteriorating) — lithium toxicity can be life-threatening, can occur even with a level in range in an unwell patient, and severe cases may need haemodialysis — rather than continuing lithium, waiting for a routine test or sending her home; thyroid function and calcium belong to the later monitoring review (NICE CG185, 2014). Identify and address the precipitants: dehydration from the D&V is the obvious one, but review interacting drugs that raise lithium (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and thiazide diuretics) and low salt, stopping offenders and correcting fluid/salt balance. Reinforce lithium sick-day rules and safety (maintain fluids and seek advice early in dehydrating illness, avoid NSAIDs, check interactions with new medicines, know toxicity symptoms, attend regular monitoring, carry the lithium alert card and record book — NPSA/2009/PSA005). The hidden agenda is the patient rationalising it as "just the bug" and underplaying the confusion — the daughter’s concern is the key signal; take the physical emergency seriously and act, while remaining mindful of her bipolar disorder so that lithium is re-established safely with psychiatric input once recovered, given relapse risk.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG185 (bipolar disorder in adults, 2014, updated) · [2] NPSA Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2009/PSA005, Safer lithium therapy (December 2009) · [3] BNF lithium monographs · [4] NICE QS95 (bipolar disorder in adults)
knowledge.summary: A patient on lithium who becomes confused, ataxic and coarsely tremulous after vomiting and diarrhoea has lithium toxicity until a level proves otherwise. Stop the lithium, get an urgent level and renal function, and arrange same-day hospital assessment.

points.t: NICE CG185 [1] and QS95 [4]: aim for a 12-hour post-dose plasma level of 0.6–0.8 mmol/L for most people (0.8–1.0 mmol/L after a relapse on a lower level, or with subthreshold symptoms). Small rises in level can produce toxicity, and toxicity can occur at a level within the range in an unwell patient.

Lithium is cleared by the kidney alongside sodium. Vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, sweating or poor intake reduce clearance and push the level up. CG185 [1]: advise people on lithium to seek medical help if they develop diarrhoea or vomiting or become acutely ill, and to keep fluids up.

Coarse tremor (the therapeutic tremor is fine), ataxia, slurred speech, muscle twitching, drowsiness or confusion, and worsening GI upset. Severe toxicity brings seizures, arrhythmia, renal failure and coma. Her confusion and unsteadiness are neurological signs, so this is not a stay-at-home case.

Stop lithium now. Arrange same-day hospital assessment for an urgent lithium level, U&E and creatinine, and fluids; severe cases may need haemodialysis. Do not wait for a routine GP blood test while she stays at home confused. Check thyroid function and calcium as part of the monitoring review once she is safe.

BNF [3] and CG185 [1]: NSAIDs (including over-the-counter ibuprofen), ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-II receptor blockers and diuretics (especially thiazides) raise lithium levels. Ask about anything taken for the bug or for pain.

NPSA/2009/PSA005 [2]: patients on lithium should have monitoring in line with NICE CG185, reliable communication of results, and ongoing written information with a record book and alert card. CG185 [1]: level every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months (3-monthly in higher-risk groups); renal and thyroid function and calcium every 6 months.

Once she has recovered and the level and renal function are known, restart and re-check the level with her mental-health team’s advice. Stopping lithium abruptly and long-term raises the risk of relapse, so do not end it unilaterally.

dg.d: Open start; took “is the lithium relevant?” seriously and let her describe the tremor, unsteadiness and slowed thinking.
Who is with her, whether she can get to hospital safely, and how the illness is affecting her at home.
Urgent lithium level (12 hours post-dose where possible, but not delayed for timing), U&E and creatinine; thyroid function and calcium at review; drug and fluid history.
Lithium toxicity versus gastroenteritis alone, AKI, sepsis or other causes of acute confusion.
Screened for drowsiness, seizures, arrhythmia symptoms and reduced urine output; recognised neurological signs as a same-day emergency.
Named likely lithium toxicity precipitated by dehydration, in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Stopped lithium, arranged same-day hospital assessment with handover, and kept the daughter involved.
Asked about NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics; planned to restart lithium with the mental-health team’s advice.
999 triggers named; follow-up call booked; sick-day rules and alert card reinforced.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Acted on the daughter’s report of confusion and on the new, coarse character of the tremor.
Idea (“just the bug”), concern (relapse if lithium stops), expectation (something for the sickness).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — she is more muddled than she admits (her daughter is worried); fear that stopping lithium will make her bipolar relapse after years of stability — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Frances, it’s Dr Patel. Thanks for calling in on video. Before anything else, tell me how you’re feeling right now.
model.why: Opens with the patient, not a checklist

model.text: Rough. This bug’s been going a few days — sick, the runs — and now my hands are really shaky and my head feels slow. I take lithium. Is that relevant?

Yes, it’s very relevant, and I’m glad you asked. I’d like to ask a few quick questions about how you are and what you’ve been taking, then tell you what I think needs to happen today. Is that alright?
model.why: Answers her question honestly and sets a focused agenda

model.text: Okay.
How long have you had the sickness and diarrhoea, and have you managed to keep any fluids down?
model.why: Quantifies the dehydration that drives the level up

model.text: Three or four days. I’ve barely kept anything down.
And the shakiness — is it the usual fine tremor you sometimes get, or different?
model.why: Separates a coarse toxic tremor from the therapeutic fine tremor

model.text: Different. Much bigger, like I can’t hold a cup. And I’m wobbly when I walk.
You said your daughter thinks you seem confused. What has she noticed?
model.why: Picks up the daughter’s concern as the key cue

model.text: She says I’m not making sense at times. I told her it’s just the bug.
I’m really glad she said something — she may be seeing more clearly than you can at the moment. Any slurred speech, jerking or twitching of your muscles, or drowsiness that’s hard to shake off?
model.why: Screens for severe toxicity features

model.text: My head just feels slow. I don’t know about the rest.
Have you taken anything for the bug or for aches — ibuprofen or other anti-inflammatories — or started any new tablets, water tablets or blood-pressure tablets recently?
model.why: Checks for interacting drugs: NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics

model.text: Just the lithium as far as I remember. I’d have to check with my daughter what I took for the bug.
That’s fine — please bring or photograph anything you’ve taken. Have you been passing much urine?
model.why: Screens for acute kidney injury

model.text: I haven’t really noticed.
What were you hoping I could do for you today?
model.why: Elicits expectations

model.text: Something to stop the sickness, really. I thought it was only the bug.
That makes sense. Is anything else worrying you — about the lithium or about your mood?
model.why: Explores the hidden worry about her bipolar disorder

model.text: If you take me off it, I’m scared I’ll get ill again. It took years to get settled.
Thank you for telling me. That’s a real worry and I’ll come back to it, because we won’t just abandon a treatment that keeps you well.
model.why: Validates the fear of relapse before the plan

model.text: Here’s what I think. Lithium works in a narrow safe range. When you’re dehydrated from sickness and diarrhoea, your kidneys clear less of it and the level rises. The big shake, the wobbliness, the sleepiness and the muddled thinking are the signs I’d expect if your lithium level is now too high.
model.why: Explains likely lithium toxicity in plain language

model.text: So it’s not the bug?

The bug has probably caused it, but the lithium level is now the more serious problem. Because you’re confused and unsteady, I don’t want you waiting at home for a routine blood test. You need to be seen in hospital today for an urgent lithium level, kidney tests and fluids.
model.why: Recognises neurological signs as a red flag and arranges same-day assessment

model.text: Hospital? Is it that bad?

I can’t tell how high the level is without the test, and that’s exactly why. Most people recover well when it’s picked up early, but a high level can affect the kidneys and heart, so it needs checking today, not tomorrow.
model.why: Honest about uncertainty without frightening her

model.text: Please don’t take any more lithium until the hospital team tell you it’s safe. Could your daughter take you in? I’d like someone with you, and I’ll ring ahead and send a letter explaining that I’m worried about lithium toxicity.
model.why: Withholds lithium and organises a safe route with handover

model.text: I’ll ask her to take me.
Good. Take your lithium record book and alert card if you have them, and anything you’ve taken this week. Sip fluids on the way if you can keep them down.
model.why: Practical, specific instructions

model.text: And about your worry: once you’re better and the level and kidney tests are back, I’ll speak with your mental-health team about restarting the lithium safely and re-checking the level. Stopping for a few days to clear it is very different from stopping for good.
model.why: Addresses the relapse fear and plans psychiatric input

model.text: That’s a relief.

When you’re home, I’d like to go through the sick-day rules: if you’re vomiting, have diarrhoea or a fever, or can’t drink, keep fluids up and contact us early; avoid ibuprofen-type painkillers; and check with a pharmacist before any new medicine.
model.why: Plans lithium sick-day and interaction education

model.text: If before you reach hospital you become very drowsy, hard to wake, have a fit, or your heart races or feels irregular, call 999 straight away.
model.why: Named 999 triggers

model.text: Okay.
Can you or your daughter tell me back the three things you’re doing now?
model.why: Teach-back, involving the daughter

model.text: No more lithium, go to the hospital today with my book and card, and 999 if I get more sleepy or have a fit.
Exactly right. I’ll ring the hospital now and call you tomorrow to see how you are and book a review once you’re home.
model.why: Summarises and books follow-up

social.t: A confused patient on video may not give a reliable history. With her consent, involve the daughter who raised the concern, and check she can get to hospital safely.
Fear of relapse can make patients reluctant to stop lithium even briefly; name it and give a clear plan for restarting.

legal.t: Acute confusion may affect her capacity to decide about going to hospital. Assess capacity for that decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005) if she declines; here she agrees.
She should not drive while confused and unwell. Bipolar disorder has its own DVLA notification rules; check current DVLA guidance at review rather than today.

professional.t: NPSA/2009/PSA005: lithium monitoring, reliable result communication, and patient information with a record book and alert card. Review the practice recall once she recovers.
Ring ahead to the hospital and later inform the mental-health team; record the episode, precipitant and restart plan clearly (GMC Good medical practice).

community.t: Community pharmacists can check interactions before over-the-counter purchases. Bipolar UK offers peer support and information.

redFlags: Confusion, drowsiness, ataxia or coarse tremor in a patient on lithium
Reduced urine output or inability to keep fluids down
psychosocial: Who is at home and can take her to hospital
Her fear of relapse if lithium is stopped
ice: Concern: coming off lithium and becoming unwell again

playbook.diagnosis: “I think your lithium level has probably gone too high because the bug has dehydrated you. The shakiness, wobbliness and muddled thinking fit that, and it needs checking in hospital today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Lithium is like water in a bath with the plug partly out: your kidneys are the plug. When you’re dehydrated, the plug closes a bit and the level rises. We need to stop filling the bath and measure how high it is.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried that stopping lithium means getting ill again. Stopping it for a few days to let the level fall is different, and we’ll restart it safely with your mental-health team.”
management.psychosocial: Involve her daughter in getting her to hospital and in the teach-back, and give written sick-day rules once she is home.
sharedPlan: Stop lithium now; same-day hospital assessment for lithium level, U&E, creatinine and fluids
Review drugs that raise lithium (NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, diuretics)
Restart with the mental-health team once recovered; re-check level; reinforce record book and alert card
safetyNet: 999 for worsening drowsiness, fits, palpitations or collapse
GP follow-up call the next day and review after discharge

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed when the candidate treats the bug and misses the drug. The patient hands you the diagnosis in her first minute; the marks are for acting on it safely and keeping her engaged with her mental-health care.

items.fail: Answering “is the lithium relevant?” with “probably not” and prescribing an antiemetic.
items.why: “Fails to recognise a serious condition.” New coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion on lithium after D&V is toxicity until proved otherwise (NICE CG185).
items.fix: “Yes, very relevant. Dehydration can push your lithium up, and your symptoms fit that.”

items.fail: Stopping the lithium but booking a routine blood test for tomorrow while she stays at home confused.
items.why: Neurological signs mean possible severe toxicity; a delayed result leaves a confused patient unsupervised. “Management not safe” is the feedback statement.
items.fix: Same-day hospital assessment for level, U&E and fluids, with a phone handover.

items.fail: Never asking about ibuprofen, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics.
items.why: Missing the interacting drug means the next episode is likely. BNF and CG185 both list them.
items.fix: One direct question: “Have you taken anything for pain or started any water or blood-pressure tablets?”

items.fail: Talking over the daughter’s observation because the patient says she is fine.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The daughter’s account of confusion is the key cue.
items.fix: “Your daughter may see more clearly than you can right now. What has she noticed?”

items.fail: Telling her she should come off lithium for good after this.
items.why: Ignores her main concern and risks relapse; restarting needs the mental-health team.
items.fix: “We’re stopping it for now, and we’ll restart it safely with your team once you’re better.”

items.fail: Jargon — “narrow therapeutic index, reduced renal clearance” — to a muddled patient.
items.why: “Language not easily understood.” A confused patient needs short, concrete instructions.
items.fix: Three clear actions and teach-back: no more lithium, hospital today with your book and card, 999 if more drowsy.

items.fail: No safety-net and no follow-up once she is sent to hospital.
items.why: Care ends at the referral; the restart plan and sick-day education are lost.
items.fix: Name 999 triggers, ring ahead, and book a follow-up call and a post-discharge review.

Duration of D&V and fluid intake, character of the tremor, unsteadiness, confusion (daughter’s view), drowsiness, seizures, urine output, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, diuretics.
“Just the bug”, and the fear of relapse if lithium is stopped. Name the fear before the plan.

999 for worsening drowsiness, fits or palpitations. Teach-back with her daughter. Follow-up call booked and sick-day rules planned.

wordPics.fail: Treats the gastroenteritis and says to carry on the lithium; ignores the daughter’s report of confusion; books a routine blood test for next week; no question about NSAIDs or other drugs; no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Recognises possible lithium toxicity, stops the lithium, arranges an urgent level and renal function with hospital assessment, asks about interacting drugs, and gives a basic safety-net.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like a tummy bug — keep taking your tablets and drink plenty.”
avoid.instead: “Your lithium is very relevant. The sickness can push its level up, and your shakiness and muddled thinking may be the sign.”
avoid.why: Continuing lithium through toxicity is the key safety failure in this station.

avoid.dont: “We’ll book a lithium level for next week.”
avoid.instead: “Because you’re confused and unsteady, you need an urgent level and kidney tests in hospital today.”
avoid.why: Neurological signs make this a same-day emergency, not routine monitoring.

avoid.dont: “You’d better come off lithium altogether after this.”
avoid.instead: “We’ll stop it for now and restart it safely with your mental-health team once you’re well.”
avoid.why: Abrupt long-term withdrawal risks relapse and ignores her main concern.

Thank you for telling me. That’s a real worry and I’ll come back to it, because we won’t just abandon a treatment that keeps you well.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates the fear of relapse before the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Here’s what I think. Lithium works in a narrow safe range. When you’re dehydrated from sickness and diarrhoea, your kidneys clear less of it and the level rises. The big shake, the wobbliness, the sleepiness and the muddled thinking are the signs I’d expect if your lithium level is now too high.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains likely lithium toxicity in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: So it’s not the bug?

The bug has probably caused it, but the lithium level is now the more serious problem. Because you’re confused and unsteady, I don’t want you waiting at home for a routine blood test. You need to be seen in hospital today for an urgent lithium level, kidney tests and fluids.
SCA_MODELS.why: Recognises neurological signs as a red flag and arranges same-day assessment

SCA_MODELS.text: Hospital? Is it that bad?

I can’t tell how high the level is without the test, and that’s exactly why. Most people recover well when it’s picked up early, but a high level can affect the kidneys and heart, so it needs checking today, not tomorrow.
SCA_MODELS.why: Honest about uncertainty without frightening her

SCA_MODELS.text: Please don’t take any more lithium until the hospital team tell you it’s safe. Could your daughter take you in? I’d like someone with you, and I’ll ring ahead and send a letter explaining that I’m worried about lithium toxicity.
SCA_MODELS.why: Withholds lithium and organises a safe route with handover

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll ask her to take me.
Good. Take your lithium record book and alert card if you have them, and anything you’ve taken this week. Sip fluids on the way if you can keep them down.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical, specific instructions

SCA_MODELS.text: And about your worry: once you’re better and the level and kidney tests are back, I’ll speak with your mental-health team about restarting the lithium safely and re-checking the level. Stopping for a few days to clear it is very different from stopping for good.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the relapse fear and plans psychiatric input

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s a relief.

When you’re home, I’d like to go through the sick-day rules: if you’re vomiting, have diarrhoea or a fever, or can’t drink, keep fluids up and contact us early; avoid ibuprofen-type painkillers; and check with a pharmacist before any new medicine.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plans lithium sick-day and interaction education

SCA_MODELS.text: If before you reach hospital you become very drowsy, hard to wake, have a fit, or your heart races or feels irregular, call 999 straight away.
SCA_MODELS.why: Named 999 triggers

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay.
Can you or your daughter tell me back the three things you’re doing now?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back, involving the daughter

SCA_MODELS.text: No more lithium, go to the hospital today with my book and card, and 999 if I get more sleepy or have a fit.
Exactly right. I’ll ring the hospital now and call you tomorrow to see how you are and book a review once you’re home.
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises and books follow-up

SCA_STEM.name: Frances Doyle
pmh: Long-term lithium therapy (lithium monitoring recall on the practice register)
meds: Lithium (long-term; preparation and dose as on the repeat record)
SCA_STEM.recent: Several days of vomiting and diarrhoea, now shaky, unsteady and “muddled”. Her daughter has noticed confusion.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: “I’ve had a sickness bug and now I’m shaky — I’m on lithium, is that relevant?”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG185 (bipolar disorder in adults, 2014, updated) · [2] NPSA Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2009/PSA005, Safer lithium therapy (December 2009) · [3] BNF lithium monographs · [4] NICE QS95 (bipolar disorder in adults)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A patient on lithium who becomes confused, ataxic and coarsely tremulous after vomiting and diarrhoea has lithium toxicity until a level proves otherwise. Stop the lithium, get an urgent level and renal function, and arrange same-day hospital assessment.

points.t: NICE CG185 [1] and QS95 [4]: aim for a 12-hour post-dose plasma level of 0.6–0.8 mmol/L for most people (0.8–1.0 mmol/L after a relapse on a lower level, or with subthreshold symptoms). Small rises in level can produce toxicity, and toxicity can occur at a level within the range in an unwell patient.

Lithium is cleared by the kidney alongside sodium. Vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, sweating or poor intake reduce clearance and push the level up. CG185 [1]: advise people on lithium to seek medical help if they develop diarrhoea or vomiting or become acutely ill, and to keep fluids up.

Coarse tremor (the therapeutic tremor is fine), ataxia, slurred speech, muscle twitching, drowsiness or confusion, and worsening GI upset. Severe toxicity brings seizures, arrhythmia, renal failure and coma. Her confusion and unsteadiness are neurological signs, so this is not a stay-at-home case.

Stop lithium now. Arrange same-day hospital assessment for an urgent lithium level, U&E and creatinine, and fluids; severe cases may need haemodialysis. Do not wait for a routine GP blood test while she stays at home confused. Check thyroid function and calcium as part of the monitoring review once she is safe.

BNF [3] and CG185 [1]: NSAIDs (including over-the-counter ibuprofen), ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-II receptor blockers and diuretics (especially thiazides) raise lithium levels. Ask about anything taken for the bug or for pain.

NPSA/2009/PSA005 [2]: patients on lithium should have monitoring in line with NICE CG185, reliable communication of results, and ongoing written information with a record book and alert card. CG185 [1]: level every 3 months for the first year, then every 6 months (3-monthly in higher-risk groups); renal and thyroid function and calcium every 6 months.

Once she has recovered and the level and renal function are known, restart and re-check the level with her mental-health team’s advice. Stopping lithium abruptly and long-term raises the risk of relapse, so do not end it unilaterally.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; took “is the lithium relevant?” seriously and let her describe the tremor, unsteadiness and slowed thinking.
Who is with her, whether she can get to hospital safely, and how the illness is affecting her at home.
Acted on the daughter’s report of confusion and on the new, coarse character of the tremor.
Idea (“just the bug”), concern (relapse if lithium stops), expectation (something for the sickness).
Urgent lithium level (12 hours post-dose where possible, but not delayed for timing), U&E and creatinine; thyroid function and calcium at review; drug and fluid history.
Lithium toxicity versus gastroenteritis alone, AKI, sepsis or other causes of acute confusion.
Screened for drowsiness, seizures, arrhythmia symptoms and reduced urine output; recognised neurological signs as a same-day emergency.
Named likely lithium toxicity precipitated by dehydration, in plain words.
Stopped lithium, arranged same-day hospital assessment with handover, and kept the daughter involved.
Asked about NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics; planned to restart lithium with the mental-health team’s advice.
999 triggers named; follow-up call booked; sick-day rules and alert card reinforced.

social.t: A confused patient on video may not give a reliable history. With her consent, involve the daughter who raised the concern, and check she can get to hospital safely.
Fear of relapse can make patients reluctant to stop lithium even briefly; name it and give a clear plan for restarting.

legal.t: Acute confusion may affect her capacity to decide about going to hospital. Assess capacity for that decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005) if she declines; here she agrees.
She should not drive while confused and unwell. Bipolar disorder has its own DVLA notification rules; check current DVLA guidance at review rather than today.

professional.t: NPSA/2009/PSA005: lithium monitoring, reliable result communication, and patient information with a record book and alert card. Review the practice recall once she recovers.
Ring ahead to the hospital and later inform the mental-health team; record the episode, precipitant and restart plan clearly (GMC Good medical practice).

community.t: Community pharmacists can check interactions before over-the-counter purchases. Bipolar UK offers peer support and information.

redFlags: Confusion, drowsiness, ataxia or coarse tremor in a patient on lithium
Reduced urine output or inability to keep fluids down
psychosocial: Who is at home and can take her to hospital
Her fear of relapse if lithium is stopped
ice: Concern: coming off lithium and becoming unwell again

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “I think your lithium level has probably gone too high because the bug has dehydrated you. The shakiness, wobbliness and muddled thinking fit that, and it needs checking in hospital today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Lithium is like water in a bath with the plug partly out: your kidneys are the plug. When you’re dehydrated, the plug closes a bit and the level rises. We need to stop filling the bath and measure how high it is.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried that stopping lithium means getting ill again. Stopping it for a few days to let the level fall is different, and we’ll restart it safely with your mental-health team.”
management.psychosocial: Involve her daughter in getting her to hospital and in the teach-back, and give written sick-day rules once she is home.
sharedPlan: Stop lithium now; same-day hospital assessment for lithium level, U&E, creatinine and fluids
Review drugs that raise lithium (NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, diuretics)
Restart with the mental-health team once recovered; re-check level; reinforce record book and alert card
safetyNet: 999 for worsening drowsiness, fits, palpitations or collapse
GP follow-up call the next day and review after discharge

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed when the candidate treats the bug and misses the drug. The patient hands you the diagnosis in her first minute; the marks are for acting on it safely and keeping her engaged with her mental-health care.

items.fail: Answering “is the lithium relevant?” with “probably not” and prescribing an antiemetic.
items.why: “Fails to recognise a serious condition.” New coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion on lithium after D&V is toxicity until proved otherwise (NICE CG185).
items.fix: “Yes, very relevant. Dehydration can push your lithium up, and your symptoms fit that.”

items.fail: Stopping the lithium but booking a routine blood test for tomorrow while she stays at home confused.
items.why: Neurological signs mean possible severe toxicity; a delayed result leaves a confused patient unsupervised. “Management not safe” is the feedback statement.
items.fix: Same-day hospital assessment for level, U&E and fluids, with a phone handover.

items.fail: Never asking about ibuprofen, ACE inhibitors, ARBs or diuretics.
items.why: Missing the interacting drug means the next episode is likely. BNF and CG185 both list them.
items.fix: One direct question: “Have you taken anything for pain or started any water or blood-pressure tablets?”

items.fail: Talking over the daughter’s observation because the patient says she is fine.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The daughter’s account of confusion is the key cue.
items.fix: “Your daughter may see more clearly than you can right now. What has she noticed?”

items.fail: Telling her she should come off lithium for good after this.
items.why: Ignores her main concern and risks relapse; restarting needs the mental-health team.
items.fix: “We’re stopping it for now, and we’ll restart it safely with your team once you’re better.”

items.fail: Jargon — “narrow therapeutic index, reduced renal clearance” — to a muddled patient.
items.why: “Language not easily understood.” A confused patient needs short, concrete instructions.
items.fix: Three clear actions and teach-back: no more lithium, hospital today with your book and card, 999 if more drowsy.

items.fail: No safety-net and no follow-up once she is sent to hospital.
items.why: Care ends at the referral; the restart plan and sick-day education are lost.
items.fix: Name 999 triggers, ring ahead, and book a follow-up call and a post-discharge review.
